messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable, Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi had been a chef in the United States for several years, but the event that haunted him belonged to the road he fled as a refugee in South Asia, where a convoy was hit and the noise of the impact, the shouting, and the sight of people with torn, bleeding skin had never really left him. In the aftermath, he had been the one moving between frightened bodies, and he still carried the sense that he had not done enough to stop what happened or help the people who died. When he tried to describe it later, the story broke apart; he could point to fragments, but the frightening moment itself seemed to sit in him without words. At other times he could picture it with a strange blankness, as if it had happened to someone else, and then the numbness would crack into overwhelming grief. Those memories fed the beliefs he had come to live with: that he would never forgive himself for not doing more, that he should feel guilty for surviving when others did not, and that the experience had permanently changed him for the worse.

In the years since, those appraisals began shaping everything else. Ravi became extremely vigilant, especially in public places and at work, where he watched the door, the windows, and the people around him while he chopped vegetables or moved between the stove and the service line. He always identified escape routes before he could feel comfortable anywhere, and open or exposed spaces made him feel unprotected, so he chose seats near walls, kept to the edge of rooms, and avoided broad parking lots or plazas whenever he could. Part of that was a practical response to how easily reminders caught him off guard: ambulances slicing past with sirens, a colleague casually discussing a car accident, or the flash of a wound on a customer or coworker could turn his attention rigid and pull him back into the old fear. But those same reminders also made his mind race with the belief that danger could return without warning and that he would be helpless in the moment. When he noticed those signs, he became more guarded, more watchful, and more intent on finding a way out before he let himself settle.

Ravi also tried to manage the fear in ways that made immediate sense to him but kept the pattern going. In places where he felt threatened, he became overly compliant, smiling too quickly, agreeing too readily, and keeping his voice soft so no one would challenge him. Around police or military uniforms, or even the sight of weapons, he pulled back and tried to disappear into the background. He had come to believe that if he stayed small, stayed agreeable, and avoided anything that looked like force, he might reduce the chance of being trapped again. Yet those choices only deepened his sense that he was no longer the man he had been. The more he arranged his life around danger, the more he felt his character had been altered, and that conviction pushed his guilt harder: he blamed himself for failing before and now blamed himself for living in fear. At work, he began turning down opportunities that would require him to step into the dining room during crowded events or to assist in outdoor catering jobs in open spaces, which affected his standing with his employer and left him increasingly isolated.

The same efforts also changed the way his memories came back. When he was scanning exits, avoiding uniforms, or shrinking himself to keep others calm, the event returned in pieces that were harder to place into a coherent story. He could see flashes of injuries, hear an ambulance in the distance, or feel the old helplessness, but the more he pushed himself to stay safe, the more the memory seemed to retreat into wordless fragments and numb, stranger-like scenes. Even brief reminders now seemed potent because they had become linked to his own rules for safety and blame. Seeing an ambulance outside the restaurant, hearing coworkers mention a crash, or noticing a customer’s bandaged arm did not only jar him; they confirmed, in his mind, that danger was still nearby and that his failure and survival still defined him. That belief kept his concentration poor, his body tense, and his attention constantly scanning for the next threat.

By the time he sought help, Ravi was exhausted by the effort of staying ahead of what frightened him. He had noticed that the world was shrinking around his routines at work and in daily life, and that his fear of ambulances, accident talk, visible wounds, uniforms, and open spaces was making him more isolated and less able to concentrate on the job he depended on. What brought him in was the sense that the cycle was tightening and that he could no longer tell whether he was protecting himself or living as if the danger had already taken over. He was afraid that if he kept going this way, he would lose the rest of his confidence and maybe his work, but he also hoped that if he could finally make sense of the memories and the guilt, he might stop living every day as though he were still on that road.
